equation_request.abstract: The effects of imperfect gate operations in implementation of Shor's prime factorization algorithm are investigated. The gate imperfections may be classified into three categories: the systematic error, the random error, and the one with combined errors. It is found that Shor's algorithm is robust against the systematic errors but is vulnerable to the random errors. Error threshold is given to the algorithm for a given number N to be factorized.

specification.problem: Quantify how imperfect (systematically biased and randomly fluctuating) gate operations degrade Shor's order-finding/factoring algorithm, and determine, for a given N, an error threshold below which the algorithm still succeeds with acceptable probability.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Single smallest useful instance: order finding for N=15 with base a=7 (order r=4), using an n=4 qubit work register and a t=8 qubit control register, with the standard QFT-based period-finding circuit. Imperfections are modeled only on the single-qubit rotation gates of the (inverse) QFT as (i) a systematic fractional over-rotation and (ii) independent Gaussian random phase errors; the figure of merit is the probability of measuring an outcome that yields the correct order via continued fractions. Outside scope: the paper's actual error model and which gates it perturbs, its 'combined error' category, its specific threshold values and scaling with N, imperfections in the modular-exponentiation network, and any decoherence model.

symbols.meaning: Odd composite integer to be factored
Randomly chosen base coprime to N
Multiplicative order of a modulo N
Number of work-register qubits, n=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil
Ideal rotation angle of controlled-phase gate R_k in the QFT, \theta_k=2\pi/2^k
Systematic (fixed, reproducible) fractional over-rotation of every gate angle
Random phase error on the j-th gate application
symbols.domain: Real, i.i.d. Gaussian with zero mean and standard deviation \sigma

symbols.meaning: Probability that the measured control-register outcome yields the correct order r by continued fractions
Error threshold: largest random-error strength for which P_succ stays above a chosen fraction of its ideal value

equations.label: Ideal order-finding state before inverse QFT
equations.description: State of the control and work registers after Hadamards on the control register and the controlled modular-exponentiation network, with x encoded in binary (qubit 0 = least significant bit).
equations.justification: Standard Shor order-finding construction; the abstract names Shor's algorithm but does not state this relation.
assumptions: Modular-exponentiation network is implemented perfectly (only QFT gates are perturbed in this scope).

equations.label: Ideal inverse quantum Fourier transform
equations.latex: \mathrm{QFT}^{-1}|x\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{Q}}\sum_{y=0}^{Q-1}e^{-2\pi i xy/Q}|y\rangle,\quad \text{built from } H \text{ and } R_{k}=\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{i\theta_{k}}),\ \theta_{k}=\frac{2\pi}{2^{k}}
equations.description: Inverse QFT on the control register decomposed into Hadamards and controlled phase rotations R_k; these are the gates whose angles are perturbed in this scope.
equations.justification: Textbook QFT decomposition used to define the gate set subject to imperfections.

equations.label: Systematic gate error model
equations.description: Every controlled rotation is over- or under-rotated by the same reproducible fractional amount; the perturbed circuit is still unitary and deterministic.
equations.justification: The abstract names a 'systematic error' category but does not define it; a fixed fractional over-rotation is a minimal concrete model consistent with that name.
assumptions: Error is identical on every gate and on every run.

equations.label: Random gate error model
equations.description: Each gate application receives an independent zero-mean Gaussian phase error; observables are averaged over the error ensemble.
equations.justification: The abstract names a 'random error' category without specifying its distribution; i.i.d. Gaussian angle noise is a minimal concrete model.
assumptions: Gaussian distribution and independence across gates are chosen, not sourced.

equations.label: Success probability figure of merit
equations.description: Probability, averaged over random errors, that the measured outcome y lies in the set S_r of outcomes from which the continued-fraction expansion of y/Q recovers the true order r. |psi_c> is the reduced control state after the work register is traced out/measured.
equations.abstract_quote: Shor's algorithm is robust against the systematic errors but is vulnerable to the random errors
equations.justification: Comparing robustness across error types requires a scalar performance metric; the probability of recovering the correct order is the natural one, though the abstract does not state which metric is used.
assumptions: The paper may use a different metric (e.g., fidelity of the output distribution).

equations.label: Error threshold definition
equations.description: Threshold on the random-error strength for a given N, defined as the largest sigma for which the success probability remains at least a fixed fraction kappa of its ideal value.
equations.abstract_quote: Error threshold is given to the algorithm for a given number N to be factorized.
equations.justification: The abstract states a threshold depending on N exists but gives neither its definition nor values; this is one concrete operationalization with kappa as a free choice.
assumptions: The threshold is defined on the random-error strength because the abstract says the algorithm is vulnerable to random errors.

registers.name: control
registers.role: Phase-estimation register; holds superposition over exponents x and is Fourier-transformed and measured. Qubit 0 is the least significant bit of x.

registers.name: work
registers.role: Holds a^x mod N after controlled modular multiplication; initialized to |1>.

specification.initial_state: |0\rangle^{\otimes t}_{c}\otimes|1\rangle_{w} = |0\ldots0\rangle_{c}|0001\rangle_{w} (binary 1 in the work register, LSB = qubit 0)

steps.description: Apply H to each control qubit and the controlled-U^{2^j} modular multiplications (U|y>=|a y mod N>) to produce the ideal entangled state.
Apply the inverse QFT to the control register using the H and R_k decomposition.
Replace each R_k by its imperfect version: systematic over-rotation (case A), random Gaussian phase error (case B), or both (combined case, outside the scoped equations).
Measure the control register and compute the success probability, averaging over random-error samples for cases B.
Sweep epsilon and sigma; identify the error threshold for N=15 from the decay of P_succ.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of all t control qubits, giving integer y in [0, Q-1]; repeated over many runs (and over independent random-error samples) to estimate the outcome distribution.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Continued-fraction expansion of y/Q to obtain a candidate denominator r'; verify a^{r'} ≡ 1 (mod N); if r' is even and a^{r'/2} ≢ -1 (mod N), output gcd(a^{r'/2} ± 1, N). For N=15, a=7: r=4 and the factors are gcd(48,15)=3 and gcd(50,15)=5. P_succ is estimated as the fraction of outcomes in S_r.
assumptions: Instance choice N=15, a=7, t=8, n=4 is a smallest-useful selection, not sourced from the abstract.
Only the QFT controlled-phase gates are perturbed; Hadamards and the modular-exponentiation network are ideal.
Systematic error modeled as a uniform fractional over-rotation; random error modeled as i.i.d. Gaussian angle noise.
Success probability of recovering the true order is used as the performance metric.
Threshold defined via a fixed fraction kappa of the ideal success probability.
missing_information: The paper's precise definition of systematic, random, and combined gate errors (which gates, which parameters, which distributions).
Whether errors are applied to the modular-exponentiation gates, the QFT, or both.
The performance metric actually used and the quantitative definition of the error threshold.
Numerical threshold values and their dependence on N.
Any analytic result explaining robustness to systematic errors (e.g., coherent error cancellation) versus vulnerability to random errors.
